results.name: magnitude_scaled_neighbour_breadth
results.description: In multi-example sets, among non-example targets 4-15 from their nearest example and sharing no final digit with any example, yes-rate when the nearest example is >= 50 minus when it is <= 30; observed above the null means people's numeric neighbourhoods widen with magnitude (Weber-like) more than the model's compressed number line predicts, below means the model over-widens them at large magnitudes.
results.code:
# name: magnitude_scaled_neighbour_breadth
# description: In multi-example sets, among non-example targets 4-15 from their nearest example and sharing no final digit with any example, yes-rate when the nearest example is >= 50 minus when it is <= 30; observed above the null means people's numeric neighbourhoods widen with magnitude (Weber-like) more than the model's compressed number line predicts, below means the model over-widens them at large magnitudes.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    diff = np.abs(E - t[:, None])
    dist = np.nanmin(diff, axis=1)
    nearest = E[np.arange(len(t)), np.nanargmin(np.where(np.isnan(diff), np.inf, diff), axis=1)]
    share_fd = np.any(np.mod(E, 10) == np.mod(t, 10)[:, None], axis=1)
    m = (n >= 2) & (dist >= 4) & (dist <= 15) & (~share_fd)
    a, b = m & (nearest >= 50), m & (nearest <= 30)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: prime_set_prime_targets
results.description: In sets of 2+ examples that are all prime, among odd non-example targets more than 3 from every example and sharing no final digit with any example, yes-rate for prime minus non-prime targets; observed above the null means people use the 'primes' rule more than the model, below means the model over-weights it.
results.code:
# name: prime_set_prime_targets
# description: In sets of 2+ examples that are all prime, among odd non-example targets more than 3 from every example and sharing no final digit with any example, yes-rate for prime minus non-prime targets; observed above the null means people use the 'primes' rule more than the model, below means the model over-weights it.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    primes = np.array([n > 1 and all(n % a for a in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1)) for n in range(101)])
    Ei = np.nan_to_num(E, nan=0).astype(int)
    valid = ~np.isnan(E)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    all_prime = np.all(primes[Ei] | ~valid, axis=1) & (n >= 2)
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(E - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    share_fd = np.any(np.mod(E, 10) == (t % 10)[:, None], axis=1)
    m = all_prime & (~is_ex) & (t % 2 == 1) & (dist > 3) & (~share_fd)
    a, b = m & primes[t], m & ~primes[t]
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: lag1_residual_dependence
results.description: Within-participant correlation between consecutive trials' residual responses (rating minus cell yes-rate minus the participant's mean residual); observed above the null means responses perseverate (a yes makes the next yes more likely) beyond what the trial-independent model produces, below means people alternate.
results.code:
# name: lag1_residual_dependence
# description: Within-participant correlation between consecutive trials' residual responses (rating minus cell yes-rate minus the participant's mean residual); observed above the null means responses perseverate (a yes makes the next yes more likely) beyond what the trial-independent model produces, below means people alternate.
def test_statistic(df):
    ti = df["trial_index"].to_numpy()
    pid = (ti == 0).cumsum()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    key = df["number_set"].astype(str) + "|" + df["target"].astype(str)
    res = r - pd.Series(r).groupby(key.to_numpy()).transform("mean").to_numpy()
    res = res - pd.Series(res).groupby(pid).transform("mean").to_numpy()
    ok = (pid[1:] == pid[:-1]) & (np.diff(ti) == 1)
    a, b = res[1:][ok], res[:-1][ok]
    if a.std() == 0 or b.std() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.corrcoef(a, b)[0, 1])

results.name: single_example_shared_digit
results.description: In single-example sets with a two-digit example, among non-example targets more than 5 away, yes-rate for targets sharing any digit with the example minus targets sharing none; observed above the null means a lone example's digits drive generalization more than the model's digit rules predict, below means the model over-applies digit rules to one example.
results.code:
# name: single_example_shared_digit
# description: In single-example sets with a two-digit example, among non-example targets more than 5 away, yes-rate for targets sharing any digit with the example minus targets sharing none; observed above the null means a lone example's digits drive generalization more than the model's digit rules predict, below means the model over-applies digit rules to one example.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    single = ~s.str.contains(",").to_numpy()
    x = pd.to_numeric(s.where(single, "0"), errors="coerce").fillna(0).astype(int).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    def digits(v):
        out = np.zeros((len(v), 10), dtype=bool)
        idx = np.arange(len(v))
        out[idx, v % 10] = True
        out[idx[v >= 10], (v[v >= 10] // 10) % 10] = True
        out[idx[v == 100], 1] = True
        return out
    share = np.any(digits(x) & digits(t), axis=1)
    m = single & (x >= 10) & (x <= 99) & (t != x) & (np.abs(t - x) > 5)
    a, b = m & share, m & ~share
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: participant_breadth_dispersion
results.description: SD across participants (segmented by trial_index resets) of each participant's mean residual yes (rating minus the (set, target) cell's yes-rate across all participants); observed above the null means individuals differ in overall generalization breadth more than the single-parameter-set model produces, below means the model over-disperses participants.
results.code:
# name: participant_breadth_dispersion
# description: SD across participants (segmented by trial_index resets) of each participant's mean residual yes (rating minus the (set, target) cell's yes-rate across all participants); observed above the null means individuals differ in overall generalization breadth more than the single-parameter-set model produces, below means the model over-disperses participants.
def test_statistic(df):
    pid = (df["trial_index"].to_numpy() == 0).cumsum()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    key = df["number_set"].astype(str) + "|" + df["target"].astype(str)
    cell_mean = pd.Series(r).groupby(key.to_numpy()).transform("mean").to_numpy()
    res = pd.Series(r - cell_mean).groupby(pid).mean()
    return float(res.std(ddof=0))

results.name: shared_contained_digit_units
results.description: In 2-4 example sets where every example contains a common digit d but not all end in it, among non-example targets more than 5 from every example, yes-rate for targets ending in such a d minus targets containing no such d; observed above the null means people extend a shared contained digit into the units place more than the model's contains/ends-in rules predict, below means the model over-produces it.
results.code:
# name: shared_contained_digit_units
# description: In 2-4 example sets where every example contains a common digit d but not all end in it, among non-example targets more than 5 from every example, yes-rate for targets ending in such a d minus targets containing no such d; observed above the null means people extend a shared contained digit into the units place more than the model's contains/ends-in rules predict, below means the model over-produces it.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(E)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    Ei = np.nan_to_num(E, nan=-1).astype(int)
    common = np.zeros((len(t), 10), dtype=bool)
    endsall = np.zeros((len(t), 10), dtype=bool)
    tcont = np.zeros((len(t), 10), dtype=bool)
    for d in range(10):
        has = (np.mod(Ei, 10) == d) | (((Ei // 10) % 10 == d) & (Ei >= 10)) | ((Ei == 100) & (d in (0, 1)))
        common[:, d] = np.all(has | ~valid, axis=1)
        endsall[:, d] = np.all((np.mod(Ei, 10) == d) | ~valid, axis=1)
        tcont[:, d] = (t % 10 == d) | (((t // 10) % 10 == d) & (t >= 10)) | ((t == 100) & (d in (0, 1)))
    cd = common & ~endsall
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(E - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    m = cd.any(axis=1) & (n >= 2) & (~is_ex) & (dist > 5)
    unit_hit = cd[np.arange(len(t)), t % 10]
    none = ~np.any(cd & tcont, axis=1)
    a, b = m & unit_hit, m & none
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: digit_reversal_target
results.description: Among non-example two-digit targets more than 3 from every example and sharing no final digit with any example, yes-rate for targets that are the digit reversal of an example (e.g. 43 after 34) minus the yes-rate for the other such targets in the same multi-example sets; observed above the null means people treat digit reversals as similar beyond the model's rules, below means the model over-produces them.
results.code:
# name: digit_reversal_target
# description: Among non-example two-digit targets more than 3 from every example and sharing no final digit with any example, yes-rate for targets that are the digit reversal of an example (e.g. 43 after 34) minus the yes-rate for the other such targets in the same multi-example sets; observed above the null means people treat digit reversals as similar beyond the model's rules, below means the model over-produces them.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(E - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    share_fd = np.any(np.mod(E, 10) == np.mod(t, 10)[:, None], axis=1)
    ti = t.astype(int)
    rev = np.where((ti >= 10) & (ti <= 99), (ti % 10) * 10 + ti // 10, -1).astype(float)
    is_rev = np.any(E == rev[:, None], axis=1) & (rev != t) & (ti % 10 != 0)
    base = (~is_ex) & (n >= 2) & (ti >= 10) & (ti <= 99) & (dist > 3) & (~share_fd)
    hasrev = pd.Series(is_rev & base).groupby(df["number_set"].to_numpy()).transform("any").to_numpy()
    m = base & hasrev
    a, b = m & is_rev, m & (~is_rev)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: within_set_target_dispersion
results.description: Mean, over sets with at least 5 distinct non-example targets, of the SD across those targets of each target's yes-rate; observed above the null means people's generalization within a set is more all-or-none across targets (sharper concept boundaries) than the model, below means people's gradients are flatter/more graded than the model predicts.
results.code:
# name: within_set_target_dispersion
# description: Mean, over sets with at least 5 distinct non-example targets, of the SD across those targets of each target's yes-rate; observed above the null means people's generalization within a set is more all-or-none across targets (sharper concept boundaries) than the model, below means people's gradients are flatter/more graded than the model predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    d = df.loc[~is_ex, ["number_set", "target", "rating"]]
    cm = d.groupby(["number_set", "target"])["rating"].mean().reset_index()
    g = cm.groupby("number_set")["rating"].agg(["std", "size"])
    g = g[g["size"] >= 5]
    if len(g) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(g["std"].mean())
